title: Negromancy public claim ledger
notes: This public ledger is independent of the private manuscript. Source claims, project interpretations, and speculative hypotheses are distinct. Links were checked against publisher or institutional descriptions; this ledger is not a verified full-text source audit.

claims.claim: Obeah was criminalized in colonial Jamaica in 1760 after a major rebellion of enslaved Africans.
claims.limit: Historian account; a verified transcription of the statute is not hosted here.

claims.claim: Vincent Brown's digital project maps the 1760–61 Jamaican rebellion and examines the limits of mapping it.
claims.limit: Interpretive cartography, not exhaustive underlying data.

claims.claim: The National Library of Jamaica provides digitized primary resources on the 1831 and 1865 uprisings.
claims.limit: Separate events; no causal continuity presumed.

claims.claim: Diana Taylor argues for embodied performance as a medium of knowledge transmission.
claims.limit: Does not make every performance testimony accurate.

claims.claim: Saidiya Hartman analyzes the silences and violence of the archive of Atlantic slavery.
claims.limit: Cannot reconstruct unrecorded lives as documented facts.

claims.claim: Within institutions, classification can organize authority, visibility and permitted action.
claims.limit: Project inference; show specific mechanisms in each case.

claims.claim: Tracing who bears the cost of an arrangement may help reveal how it is maintained.
claims.limit: Not a theory endorsed or proven by these authors.

claims.claim: Relations obscured or displaced may become active through later embodied, institutional or sacred encounters.
claims.limit: Historical continuity and causation must be tested separately; no supernatural mechanism established.

claims.claim: Fetish-space-time may help examine how produced relations appear as properties of bodies, objects, places and times.
claims.limit: Author-developed hypothesis without a validated general explanatory mechanism.
